They come out of the boils of the SlugPox, they arrive with a crude and rowdy culture already assembled, and they throw themselves at the demons with the enthusiasm of people who cannot believe their luck at being included.

beats.headline: Credit to Kandy Newton
beats.text: System message: the Sepsis Whore of the Blood Sultanate has fallen, and credit for the kill goes to Kandy "Bigs" Newton of the Princess Posse. She is a level-29 sluggalette the size of a bulldog, with wisps of pink hair and a hatchet growing out of the top of her head, and she came out of Carl's back when his slugpox broke loose. The Blood Sultanate is defeated, its assets passing to Donut and Katia and on to the Posse. Her next moves are to swing at Samantha and to try to bury the hatchet in Baroness Victory's leg, which it passes straight through.

beats.headline: The code
beats.text: Bigs, sitting on Dong's head and swinging her hatchet at Carl, lays out the sluggalo code: unity, support, family, and kneecapping. By that standard Carl has provided none of the four, which in her reckoning makes him the problem. He agrees with her, which she was not expecting. They settle on a word for what people are when they keep helping each other anyway, and the word is Real Gs. She slimes off, leaving an orange streak on Dong's head, and tells Carl she is not the one he owes an apology.

beats.headline: Lil' Mello Haze
beats.text: The boil on Carl's back bursts in the Vendor Village and delivers a level thirty slug named Lil' Mello Haze, higher level than Bigs but smaller, on account of Carl currently being a dachshund. He wears a backward baseball cap hanging off his eye sockets and has a mace head for a tail instead of the usual hatchet. He greets his father as daddy man, is called to heel, ignores it, and wanders off in the opposite direction. The father's barking does not help.

beats.headline: Down onto the stands
beats.text: The bay doors of the Reaver transport open over the judging stands and the sluggalos come down on the audience: bankers, politicians and elites, masked, bound and unable to fight back. The smallest of the small, the lowest form of dungeon NPC, slaughtering them one by one. It is the last thing on the Vengeance float, and it was planned. Bigs calls it unity, support, family and kneecapping.

tagline.text: Half human and, the System says, half human. Bred for strength and dexterity, which is to say for driving trains.
Half human, and, where the horse ought to be, also half human. The System calls it one of the weirdest of the ’taurs and offers no defence of the design.

beats.headline: Of all the ’taurs, this one
beats.text: Centaurs, bisontaurs, rhinotaurs: the dungeon has a long catalogue of things joined at the waist to other things, and this is the entry the System itself flags as peculiar. They turn up from the fourth floor down, and they keep company with Club Vanquisher.

entities.name: Protective Shell

tagline.text: A spell that comes with a pair of boxers: a sphere no mob can enter, twenty seconds, once every thirty hours. It does not move with you.
A sphere no mob can enter, and it stays exactly where it was cast. Cast it on anything moving, and everything in its path meets a wall.

entities.description: A favorite of frontline tanks and castle guards, the expensive and rare Protective Shell spell shields the caster and anyone within the sphere from a mob's physical presence or physical attacks. This spell does not protect against magic or against non-corporeal entities. Unlike the more popular Shield spell, this spell does not move with you. This spell's area of effect remains static once cast, unimpeded by your physical surroundings.

beats.headline: Inside a pair of boxers
beats.text: A boss box yields a white pair of boxers covered in little red hearts, the Enchanted BigBoi Boxers: plus two Constitution, and the wearer may cast a level-fifteen Protective Shell once every thirty hours. No mana; take the boxers off and the spell goes with them. A sphere with a radius of three metres plus half a metre per point of Intelligence, lasting twenty seconds. Mordecai had it during his own crawl and starts to explain its fantastic secondary effect, when an admin warning cuts him off.

beats.headline: A dog at the end of its leash
beats.text: First cast, in a hallway, with a rage elemental coming for the residents. The glowing half-sphere fills the corridor floor to ceiling, and the monster flies back like a charging dog reaching the end of its leash. It charges again; its badger head gets through, but its claws cannot. Crawler Carl's ears pop as he runs out of the area toward the safe room. Twenty seconds, and he spent five of them being dumbfounded that it worked.

beats.headline: Lions off a bug zapper
beats.text: Six mold lions pounce at once in a dark street. Crawler Carl slams the shell down as Crawler Donut's Confusing Fog billows out, and the lions bounce off it like fireflies off a bug zapper, each ricocheting in a different direction, howling. It holds long enough for Carl to punch into a lion's chest with his gauntlet and pull its heart out. The shell fizzles just as the reanimated lion gets back to its feet.

beats.headline: The boxers, upgraded
beats.text: An upgrade scroll goes onto the boxers. The spell itself does not change; the garment gets plus five Dexterity, plus five Intelligence, three more Constitution, and the Freeballing benefit, which permits one layer of clothing over the crotch and so rules out trousers. Mordecai calls them probably the most valuable item Crawler Carl owns. Five points of Intelligence is two and a half more metres of radius.

beats.headline: Left behind on the tracks
beats.text: The secondary effect, applied. Trapped in a speeding subway car with mobs breaking through the doors, Crawler Carl checks that the track is straight and casts. The shell ignores solid objects and stays exactly where it was cast along the track, so the train carries on through it, and it rolls down the cars, sixteen to twenty, pushing every mob before it like a bulldozer and squashing them into paste against the first surface they meet.

beats.headline: The train drives into it
beats.text: The plan for the Nightmare Express: stand on the track in the tunnel, cast the shell as the train arrives, and let Crawler Donut's Puddle Jumper take them a quarter of a mile down the line. They cut it close. The train roars through the spell, and every red-tagged monster aboard slams into its wall and is pushed backward. The train then speeds up, and they have to run for the platform.

beats.headline: The floor was the monster
beats.text: Cast on a stairway as a door explodes inward, the shell sweeps the sand off the floor of the room like a broom and uncovers glass beneath. Suddenly the whole room is red on the map. The sand is a mob, and there is no second cast today.

beats.headline: Straight down a city boss
beats.text: Swallowed along with a submarine, Crawler Carl casts in the throat of an enormous shark. The static sphere, about twelve metres across by now, shoots away as the shark swims on. He hoped for a bullet through the brain. Instead the boss stops dead, as if it had hit a wall; the top of its mouth peels back over its own eyes, teeth shatter, and the immovable spell pushes it down into the ocean floor. Grievously wounded, it is not yet dead.

beats.headline: Train the spell, upgrade the shorts
beats.text: The tier-four training room installed for Crawler Carl while he is held off the floor lists spells that come from equipment alongside the ordinary ones. Train Protective Shell there, and it is the equipment that gets upgraded: the boxers, in this case. The room also trains workshop tables without them being present, which Crawler Carl rates as its most valuable feature.

beats.headline: Straight up, not sideways
beats.text: The frog-lizard boss on the hill had a weak belly and a description hinting it should be rolled over. Crawler Carl cast too close and at the wrong angle, and the monster went straight up into the night sky instead of sideways. Crawler Donut's fireball met its stomach as it fell back down, and it landed on the shield in flames. Now, in a saferoom, the achievement catches up: Uprooted notes that a rooted-in-place boss was moved, and hopes he remembers how.

beats.headline: A crater of bugs
beats.text: A literal wave of thrashing bugs falls on Crawler Carl in the fight with a deity. He slams the shell down. Bugs, elves, dinosaurs and a few hunters rocket away in every direction. With the Intelligence he has now, the shell is huge; it leaves a crater with only crawlers and corpses in the middle, and Imani uses the gap to heal whoever she can reach.

tagline.text: Heavy metal, a frozen world, and a crawler's face with Death Challenge! stamped across it in blood. The dungeon has opened a book on how he dies.
Not a boss battle: a pop-up gambling event, at odds the AI sets. The first one put Carl's survival at fifty to one, and Borant is appealing.

beats.headline: The world freezes, the music starts
beats.text: Carl tumbles out of a portal into Trainyard E beside a glowing mantaur, a Mimic Rex's mouth opens in front of him, and the world stops. Music starts: heavy metal, bass-driven. A framed graphic of Carl's face appears in the air with Death Challenge! stamped across it, blood running from the words. The announcer promises the death of a celebrated crawler, live, and asks which lucky monster gets to kill him. Carl, frozen, has one thought about it, and it is a swear word.

beats.headline: Two contenders and a sponsor
beats.text: On the right, a level-90 Mimic Rex, city boss and crawler-killer champion of the floor with over 23,000 deaths. On the left, Grull, and for the first time on Dungeon Crawler World his sponsor: Prince Maestro of the Skull Empire, once thought dead, interviewed on screen telling the worms to try harder. The world stays frozen through the portraits while Donut gallops toward the trainyard on Mongo. Then the announcer tells everyone to get their bets in, and the world unfreezes.

beats.headline: No announcement at the end
beats.text: Grull splits the mimic in half, steps on Carl, and runs off after a second Carl who is Katia in disguise. Carl lives through the god's stamping on Mordecai's Special Brew. A mutilated mantaur, thrown into the portal with one second left on its summoning, takes the god away mid-attack. Then the music stops. There is no additional announcement, the way there usually is. There is only the chugging of a train, and a whole page of notifications.

beats.headline: What the odds were
beats.text: On Odette's couch it is explained. A Death Challenge is not a boss battle but a pop-up gambling event: viewers in systems where gambling is legal bet on outcomes, general or specific, each at its own odds. The AI put Carl's general survival at fifty to one. Plenty of viewers thought that was a good bet, and the odds slid less than you would expect. Borant has filed an appeal over how slowly the AI moved the spread. Odette made a good amount of credits.

tagline.text: Vorpal. A word a hobgoblin explosives dealer uses about a muskrat: her mother bit its head off, and you cannot do that to a vorpal muskrat without doing a little dying.
Vorpals. Whatever waits behind the Desperado Club's Do Not Enter door, released as a last resort when a demon gets loose on the middle floor.
Vorpals. A condition, not a species: deputised by the gods, drawn to demons, stronger the nearer one is, and liable to explode rather than lose.

beats.headline: One muskrat, one mother
beats.text: A hobgoblin at the Silk Road, midway through pricing hob-lobbers, mentions that she once watched her mother bite the head off a vorpal muskrat. To teach the warlord a lesson, her mother said; the daughter suspects another reason. A few minutes on, Princess Donut hopes the mother won't be biting her head off too. No danger, says the hobgoblin: she died. It was a vorpal muskrat. You can't bite the head off a vorpal muskrat without doing a little dying in the process. Nobody asks what vorpal means.

beats.headline: Fifteen things behind a door
beats.text: In a secret corridor of the Desperado Club, past fifty traps, some of them demon snares, is the abandoned practice arena of the defunct Demon Tamer's Guild, and in it fifteen red-tagged monsters nobody has identified. The paper sign on the padlocked door: Warning. Do Not Enter. Extreme, You're-Going-To-Die-In-A-Lot-Of-Pain Danger. Posted by Management. Parties have gone in. None came out. Carl, setting an ambush in that same corridor, walls the door off with two blast-resistant panels and sandbags, on a feeling.

beats.headline: The last resort
beats.text: A feral demon out of the Nothing is loose on the middle floor, eating guards, and the club cannot kill her. Astrid pulls the trigger: "I had to unleash the vorpals." Carl asks what those are. It does not matter, she says; they are going to kill everything, so flee or hide. Then she frets about what is taking them so long. Meanwhile, guards heading down that corridor keep landing on Carl's teleport traps. The vorpals won't go up to the top floor, she adds, not sounding sure.

beats.headline: Deputised by the gods
beats.text: Mordecai, asked in chat, has not seen these in a while. Vorpal is a condition, not a species. Feral means touched by the Nothing; vorpal means deputised by the gods, or better, turned into suicide bombers. Any race, sometimes hidden until a demon is near. Celestial guards and foot soldiers. The closer the demon, the stronger and angrier they get; they sense it, go to it, and draw its aggro. If one thinks it is losing, it explodes, and everybody in the room is dead with it. Stay away.

beats.headline: Carl opens his own wall
beats.text: The only thing between the vorpals and the club is the wall Carl built. So he sends a door-opening bot down the hidden hallway, programmed with a sixty-second delay to undo his own bracers and burrow through his own sandbags, and goes upstairs. Some minutes on, a buzzsaw sound rises through the floor of the strip club, and yellow fluid sprays through a hole in the boards. The demon screams a name, and a curse, and stops. The vorpals have found her.

beats.headline: Still loose downstairs
beats.text: The demon is dead and the vorpals are still tearing through the lower level. Now that they have bathed in demon blood they are supposed to dissipate back to the celestial realm, which is fine in theory and silent on timing. Crawler Carl keeps an eye on Damascus Steel, crying on the floor of the club, because Damascus is a demon class and his presence is a problem with those things still in the building.

tagline.text: T'Ghee. A card game from Allister's home planet, somewhere between chess and go fish, and part of a meditation-based religion. His Cookbook came as a deck of them.
T'Ghee totems. Plant a squad flag in something below five per cent health and it becomes a card that fights for whoever summons it. Twenty flags a squad, no refills.
T'Ghee cards. Totems, utility, snare, mystic and special. Four drawn when combat starts, one more every ten seconds, and a squad leader without spells or inventory until the deck is spent.
T'Ghee cards. The eighth floor's whole game, and a flag works on a dying crawler as well as on a monster.

beats.headline: Allister's deck of cards
beats.text: The Cookbook manifests differently for each owner. For Allister, author of the thirteenth edition, it came as a massive deck of playing cards from his home planet, for a game called T'Ghee. From the little he wrote about it, a mix of chess and go fish; also part of his people's meditation-based religion, which made it easy for him to spend hours studying the cards.

beats.headline: Two vampires in the deck
beats.text: Allister, on vampires: his culture has them too, and his T'Ghee deck contains two vampiric forms. Both represent death and the end of days. One is deliberate, thirst-based evil. The other, the Plague Bearer, is a study in how poor actions ripple through time, amplify, and doom everyone. The vampires on the floor he is writing from, he thinks, are a combination of the two. It is strange, he writes, that the traditions are so different yet the same.

beats.headline: Twenty flags a squad
beats.text: Floor announcement. Each squad leader receives twenty flags bearing a logo the system designed. Plant one in a living thing below five per cent health, noncorporeal included, and it becomes a T'Ghee totem, a minion of whoever summons it, obedient to a point depending on level and temperament. Rip the totem in two to dismiss it. Trade them, steal them. Lost flags are not replaced. Every surviving squad keeps one card when the floor collapses. Carl's breath catches: he knows the word from the Cookbook.

beats.headline: Like the stuffed animals
beats.text: Mordecai's gloss on the announcement: T'Ghee totems are like Bautista's stuffed animals, only in the form of large playing cards. Like Carl's tarot cards, actually. Reusable even when the summoned monster dies. He has seen them used a few different ways over the seasons, so they are going to have to wait for the next announcement. Carl, who has read Allister, notes that for its inventor T'Ghee was a religion and had nothing to do with capturing monsters.

beats.headline: The rules, at length
beats.text: The full rules arrive. Six totems minimum per deck. Five card types: totems, utility, snare, mystic, special. Four cards drawn when combat starts and one more every ten seconds; one discard, recharging every thirty. A squad leader in deck combat loses spells and inventory until the deck is spent, and most totems may not attack an enemy leader while enemy totems stand, so the squad guards the leader. Against an opponent holding a deck, deck combat is compulsory. Saferooms gain practice arenas, for a fee.

beats.headline: Sacred to someone
beats.text: On the road to a cemetery, Sister Ines says what she has been holding in: all of this is a mockery of their faiths and legends, the stories stripped of meaning and made shiny, holy things mixed with fictions nobody ever believed. They do not care. Crawler Carl gives her a moment, and says it is what they do. He does not say the rest aloud. The cards themselves were sacred to the aliens the idea was stolen from. They were never meant to be used like this.

beats.headline: A flag in a person
beats.text: A squad flag does not check what it is stabbed into. Sister Ines drives one into the neck of her dying friend Paz, who has just asked to be let go, and Paz becomes a card, green, common, in her hand. She looks as stunned as everyone else that it worked. Behind her, the fountain bubbles over, and two goddesses make an appearance in the realm.

beats.headline: Millions of work hours
beats.text: An achievement, at length. Borant's proposal for this season included an outline of the eighth floor as a T'Ghee card game; artists, engineers and writers spent millions of work hours designing and balancing it for thousands of players at once, and Cascadia, the executive producer, is on the edge. Most crawlers keep ending card fights before either side draws. Crawler Carl's review: a half-assed YuGiOh! ripoff duct-taped together on an Adderall bender, and no card game is fair when players draw from different pools.

beats.headline: A card called The Inevitable
beats.text: Allister again, writing about a goddess the dwarves call the Downward Spiral: an earth and water goddess who punishes those who abuse her world and the weakest in it, a trickster, jealous of mortals, forever moving nations like chess pieces. In his religion, he writes, there is a T'Ghee card that represents such a figure. It is called The Inevitable.

beats.headline: One card to keep
beats.text: Each surviving squad may keep a single card past the collapse. Princess Donut had meant it to be Lazarus or the Golden Combo, and now offers a third: a card of Paz, in case there is a way to set him free. Crawler Carl remembers what Paz said the last time he was summoned. Not that one, and not the Golden Combo either. The Paz card is ripped in half on his shoulder.

beats.headline: The Open Wound
beats.text: Allister, on the Immortality condition: an immortal's wounds heal, but make certain they heal before the condition wears off, and pair it with a Numb spell if possible, because pain without respite takes its own toll. He has a card in his T'Ghee deck, The Open Wound. She teaches that all suffering leaves scars. So the condition scares him, and he says so in writing, for whoever reads the Cookbook next.

beats.headline: A card made permanent
beats.text: Imani's eighth-floor card, Jacobus the Reverse Tooth Fairy, is out and buzzing in Carl's face. The notice says he is now permanently summoned and can no longer be used as a card, due to something Carl did. Princess Donut did not know cards could be turned real. She and Carl are both thinking of Paz, whose card they ripped, and neither says it. Could Raul be set free? Carl doubts it. This was a god thing.

relations.note: Allister's edition was a T'Ghee deck

entities.name: Containment Interface
entities.role: Bootleg interface upgrade · the AI's failsafe

tagline.text: A bootleg upgrade drunk from a homeless man's frozen coffee: access to the AI containment, and to the fuse that turns the sun nova.
Six tabs of numbers, a Fuse page with two of five conditions met, and one other button that switched all of it off. Pressed.

beats.headline: Coffee, with a finger
beats.text: Christmas morning, in a shelter, in memory. Time stops, and Paulie delivers his real message. His coffee holds a neural enhancement: Crawler Carl pushes a finger into the frozen cup and drinks. It gives access to the AI containment, and upon it to what the Mantids call the fuse, a failsafe that trips when five or six conditions are met and sends the star at the centre of the system nova. The controller lets Carl pop it himself. He dies; so does everyone. It only works in a natural interface, and the AI, says Paulie, wants it done.

beats.headline: Paulie's own opinion
beats.text: That was the pitch, Paulie says, the one he gives every day. Then the Paulie part of him speaks. Popping the fuse would disrupt the crawl for seasons, kill system leaders, and put the Mantids under a microscope. But the human in him hates wasting so many innocent lives, and direct action against the true culprits would be better. If you make this decision, be sure. It is more than a failsafe. It is the end of everything. Then a notice: Containment Interface is currently installing. A notification comes when the handshake is complete.

beats.headline: So close to the edge
beats.text: Crawler Carl thinks of Lightning Lou, the old dog at the gas station in Florida left to spend Christmas Day alone. Carl curled up beside him on the floor and contemplated his options, and came so close to the edge that it almost broke his mind to think about it. Paulie's words come back to him: be sure it's your only option. On his chest, the eye blinks.

beats.headline: The handshake completes
beats.text: In Orren's zero zone, Carl asks whether Paulie ever made it into the dungeon. No, says Orren; most of them never do, and the parts of a collective mind are often disposable. Then the notice: Containment Interface is now available for use, as a new tab. Carl changes his request and asks to be sent to the gas station with the memory ghost of the dog, and sits beside Lightning Lou with a bag of chips and a soda. I could end it all right now, he thinks.

beats.headline: Two buttons, one pressed
beats.text: There is no single Boom button. There are six tabs of numbers in a language that is not quite Syndicate standard, and the controls are for the device that installed the AI into the primal engine, not the AI itself. Carl screenshots everything. The Fuse page lists five benchmarks, two met, and a button: Override Conditions And Activate Fuse. At the end of a list sits the only other thing he can press: Disconnect Containment, which renders the failsafe inert. He weighs which hurts the Syndicate most and protects his people most, and presses Disconnect. The red dot over Earth starts to grow.

beats.headline: So close, it says
beats.text: The AI walks into Orren's office wearing Growler Gary, feet on the desk and a bottle of vodka in its hand, and brings the interface up itself. The game Carl and I played the other day, it tells Orren, when I let him install that interface. That was so close, and I felt it. Carl asks the only question that matters: would it have worked, if he had pressed the fuse button? The AI does not answer. It looks at him and laughs.

relations.note: Carl was put in that shelter by the Pacifist network

tagline.text: Flying women's heads with their organs trailing underneath. Ghost-class blood drinkers, hurt only by magic, and not dead until someone finds and destroys the body they left behind.
Women who work in the magistrate's building by day. By night their heads leave their bodies hanging upside down in a nest, and they are Remex's army.
Made from women brought to Remex: easy to control, compliant by day, and every one made is a spike of soul power for him. The ones who do not take are fed upon.

beats.headline: Three heads over an orc
beats.text: Mongo bolts into an alley, and at the end of it three disembodied female heads hover beside a tall figure with a burning hand. Long hair flaps about them; lungs and intestines hang from their necks on wet tendrils. The corpse is GumGum the orc, chest opened. Donut's Torch spell sends the heads corkscrewing into the sky, howling like banshees, and their description arrives on the way out: blood-drinking undead, a ghost-class mob hurt only by magic or magical items, and not dead-dead until the rest of the corpse is destroyed.

beats.headline: She was afraid of them
beats.text: The pub owner takes the news of GumGum badly. He knew they would get her one of these days. When she heard one at night she went into the alley anyway, saw them in the shadows, and had nightmares about one falling from the sky and not being dead. She cared about those women. Mordecai has already given his professional opinion: krasue are usually henchwomen for something else. He thinks Carl and Donut might have a lich problem.

beats.headline: Four from under the building
beats.text: Four of them emerge from underneath the building, where they have been waiting on its unoccupied first floor, and head for the roof where Carl and Donut crouch. The answer is smoke: two hobgoblin smoke curtains, and two clockwork Mongos leaping across the alley with a letter swallowed as bait. The floating heads see the dinosaurs jump before the fog closes and turn after them. Mordecai says the smoke works on these ghosts because they have a physical presence.

beats.headline: A meat locker of women
beats.text: The magistrate's bedroom is a meat locker: naked female corpses hanging upside down by the ankles. The headless ones show on the map as corpses. Thirty or more still have heads, dangling six inches below the neck, with purple energy swirling around them. Mongo's magical teeth bite through several heads. Then the rest wake up, wailing, working their heads loose, and flock through the smoke-filled room slapping at Carl with trailing organs. A lotto-ticket fireball finishes the room.

beats.headline: What Burgundy says she is
beats.text: One burned body turns back into a woman, and she explains. By day they live and work in the building as assistants and in the shops below, plucking a feather from every skyfowl who comes in for Miss Quill. At night they are his army. The women found in the alleys came to work at the Desperado Club; when Remex twists them they do not always turn, and the ones who die are fed upon, then dropped nearby by his avatars. She asks to be killed while still mortal.

beats.headline: Easy to make, easy to control
beats.text: Remex gives the reasons, in his wandering way. His wife needed help the city elves could not give. The krasue are easy to control and easy to make with the correct materials; they fly, and they are intact and compliant during the day. Making them creates a powerful spike of soul power for him. And since the raw materials come from out of town, nobody would notice she was collecting them. Donut corrects him: GumGum noticed. They were to be her lieutenants, her eyes and ears for the battle.

beats.headline: What the nest taught
beats.text: Two floors down, a crawler named Morris complains that nobody knows how to kill the ghost his party has been sent after. Carl already knows the rule, and he knows where he learned it: from the krasue creatures on the third floor. You need magic to kill ghosts. The cookbook has extensive instructions on the subject, including which bombs do the trick. Quetzalcoatlus, the ghost in question, can travel through the walls of her tomb.

tagline.text: A kind of boss Mordecai names and then sets aside: there are others, called elites, and nobody needs to worry about them just yet.
Powerful, one-of-a-kind NPCs and mobs, the non-boss hero class of the dungeon, marked on the map with a black cross. They always want to use you.
Designed, printed and imprinted to act out somebody's drama. Writers nudge them, plot armour protects them, and a crawler who walks into their story is the guest star.
Actors in secondary programs. Their owners can exert undue influence on them, which is how one arrived in a flag room wired with explosive satchels.

beats.headline: Not yet, says Mordecai
beats.text: Mordecai, freshly woken and slurring slightly, runs through the ranks of boss for two new crawlers: Neighborhood, Borough, City, Province, Country, and Floor. There are also others, he adds, but those are called elites. You won't need to worry about them just yet. Then Carl asks about what they just fought: the most common type of boss, Mordecai confirms, and now they know how to recognise its lair.

beats.headline: Meet an Elite
beats.text: The first one on the record is Tsarina Signet, half naiad, half high elf, a level-sixty summoner whose tattoos move. Her description says it outright: This is an Elite. An achievement follows. Elites are powerful, one-of-a-kind entities, the non-boss, non-divine hero class; they either want to fuck you or kill you, and always want to use you. Where there is one, there are usually more. Reward: elites now show on the map as dots with a black cross. Mordecai says to get out.

beats.headline: Printed for somebody else's show
beats.text: Mordecai explains, having already said to stay away. Thousands of elites are spread through the urban floors, and they travel between them. They are never naturals: designed, printed, imprinted with the memories their drama needs, so as far as they know this is the real world. Every storyline has its own writers, who hot patch new instructions into an elite's mind when the plot drifts. Most have thick plot armour. In their stories, a crawler is the extra, the red shirt, the guest star.

beats.headline: An elite and a city boss
beats.text: Ringmaster Grimaldi, a Pestiferous Vine as tall as the tent, is labelled This is an Elite and Level 85 City Boss in the same breath. Carl, in the bleachers with his poison ready, messages Mordecai: nobody said they could be both. On the way in he passed Apollon the Mighty, a strongman ogre selling petrified ice cream, also an elite, his dot red with a cross. Mordecai has warned him more than once that when it comes to elites, the rules don't mean shit.

beats.headline: A contract to play along
beats.text: With the vine poisoned, Carl sends Zev a message for the producers of Vengeance of the Daughter. He wants to be on their show, as a regular. If he and Donut survive the night and reach the sixth floor, he signs an exclusive agreement to complete only the elite-themed quests there that belong to their storyline. The alternative, he explains, is that he un-poisons Grimaldi with his own blood and their big night is a dud. Zev's boss patches them in.

beats.headline: A gnoll on the dance floor
beats.text: In the members-only room of the Desperado Club, three elites work the floor, white dots with crosses, each in conversation with a crawler, and an elephant-headed one leads three humans into the back. Quint the opossum explains the closed playroom: a crawler with one goat leg and two dogs froze the whole room with a spell, stole tequila, and splattered the brains of an elite gnoll who had been talking to her. Carl knows the description. Lucia Mar.

beats.headline: A coveted ninth-floor slot
beats.text: At the negotiating table, Quasar slips in an old emergency-use rule, and the kua-tin agree to keep it quiet. It guarantees Vengeance of the Daughter the equivalent of a third season. What makes that valuable is where it leads: not all secondary programs are allowed to send their elites to the ninth floor. It is a coveted reward, Quasar insists the producers are sure to leap at it, and it gives them one more reason to keep Carl alive.

beats.headline: Suggestions, not strings
beats.text: Two of Signet's were-castors insist on walking Carl and Donut back to a saferoom, and it takes Carl a minute to see why: Signet pushed them, and the showrunners pushed Signet, because Odette's show is in a few hours. Elites are not nearly as autonomous as regular NPCs. They are not controlled like robots, but showrunners may send them suggestions that make them act out of character. Carl wonders whether an elite could be made self-aware, like other NPCs, and what would happen then.

beats.headline: What the hunters leave alone
beats.text: A note in the cookbook from Drakea, 22nd edition, on the sixth floor's hunters: they avoid the elites. They are smart enough not to fight something they are not allowed to defeat easily. The trouble for crawlers is that elites are more dangerous than the hunters and much more numerous, and they should always be avoided. Some of the more powerful hunters hunt elites anyway, for the equipment and the clout. The note calls it a most dangerous game.

beats.headline: A storyline off the leash
beats.text: Miriam Dom's calls for help reach Carl late, carried by other crawlers, and the keyword in the previews explains the delay: Elite. Carl cannot help where an elite is involved. Miriam answers that the elite is dead and the quest is done; Pony killed him and was paralysed doing it. The rest follows. A vampire sickness is spreading through the dinosaurs of the forest, part of the elite's story, and he died before it could be stopped. For once, not something Carl or Donut started.

beats.headline: The main show does not share
beats.text: Carl lays it out for the other crawlers before the high elves' party. Queen Imogen is a country boss, and they are probably going to have to fight her at the end of the party. His elite quest wants to fight the same boss before or during it, which means it is doomed: the main showrunners are not going to let a secondary production hose their climax. He likes Signet. He would like to avoid going down with her. He has already told her to her face: attack when the party starts and she is dead.

beats.headline: Stay away from any elites
beats.text: A message from Quasar waits on arrival. The contract for Vengeance of the Daughter, with the third season they negotiated, is about to haunt them: Sensation Entertainment has been bought by a subsidiary of the Dream, and the new owners are demanding their season. Signet is not coming back, so whatever happens is going to be something stupid, and the new showrunners are going to try to use Carl's obligation against him. For now: stay the fuck away from any elites you see.

beats.headline: Herman the Fleet
beats.text: In the Princess Posse's castle, the only other dot on the map is an elite: Herman the Fleet, ogre strongman, a legionnaire of the Princess Posse, third brother of Grimaldi's strongmen. He is writhing at a desk. He has been waiting. Supposed to do it already. Been fighting it. Tell brother sorry. He is wearing explosive satchels. The orc adjutant steps out and kills him with an axe, then calls foul: an unlawful assassination attempt by Sensation Entertainment, exerting undue influence on one of their elites.

entities.name: Zerzura
entities.role: Spell · sends a town one floor down

tagline.text: A new spell for the Sledge, even more impressive than Bomo's teleport. Carl's lawyer suggested it, and has a story about Remex the Grand.
Takes a whole town, NPCs and buildings, one floor down. It lands somewhere awful, and whatever it squashes rises as the Children of Inpewt.
Cast by the Sledge from inside the high elf castle. The castle, the changelings and Signet's people went down to the ninth floor without the crawlers.
Cast a second time, it took Larracos and Shanty Town, NPCs and all, to the cotton fields of the twelfth floor.

beats.headline: The lawyer's idea
beats.text: Carl explains the deal for the gate. Four cretin bodyguards, and two of them got extra spells. Bomo's is Teleport to Stairwell. The Sledge's is also teleportation, and even more impressive: it was the lawyer's idea, and it is called Zerzura. Donut wants to sing the Sledge one of her new spells. Katia wants to know what it does, and does not get an answer. Carl fingers the charm on his necklace and remembers Quasar: it was glorious, shame how it ended for Remex. Everybody likes carnage when it's not them.

beats.headline: The admin gives himself away
beats.text: The negotiation, as it went. The nameless kua-tin admin from Borant pretended to hem and haw about giving Carl the four bodyguards, but the moment Quasar mentioned the Zerzura spell, he practically creamed himself. The mudskippers do not have good poker faces. Behind him, Orren the liaison grunted with amusement from his chair and said nothing once the negotiations began. Quasar winked and moved on to the next item on the list.

beats.headline: Tied to Donut's bodyguard
beats.text: Carl wants to take Donut down the stairs five days early, and Katia has an objection. The Sledge is assigned to Donut. If they go down now, he goes too, and the Zerzura spell never gets cast. Carl's answer: he promised Juice Box to do his best, not that it was a sure thing. Katia reminds him that the changelings have been risking everything to reach the Desperado Club every day in case he turns up with the plan.

beats.headline: One floor down, and no steering
beats.text: Fifteen days earlier, Quasar explained the spell. It takes a full city or town, NPCs and buildings and all, and transfers it one floor down. No mobs, no red-tagged NPCs, no stairwells or prize rooms. It is hard on the caster, so it goes into a mercenary. It can only be cast at the end of a floor, it takes five minutes, and a miscast means no second try. The town cannot be steered. It lands at random, which in practice means the worst possible place.

beats.headline: The Children of Inpewt
beats.text: The catch, per Quasar. Everything the town lands on and kills rises as a powerful revenant, the Children of Inpewt, keeping its old spells. Everyone in the town, plus the caster, is marked, and the revenants hunt the marked until they are all dead; whoever they kill turns too. On the Scolopendra levels, it skips floors: Remex sent his army from the sixth straight to the ninth, and it was slaughtered. Carl thinks of Bonnie and Skarn and Ruby, and wonders whether this is really the only choice. Then he has a crazy idea.

beats.headline: It only works on a town
beats.text: Carl hands Pearson a map with the evacuation plans on the back. They are using a spell called Zerzura, but the brambles are moving fast, and it cannot be cast for another two days. It is cast on a town, not a group of people, so the changelings need to be inside a town. The high elves have destroyed every town in the forest around them but one: the high elf castle. So that is where the changelings have to get. Pearson mentions that Juice Box told them to be careful of Carl.

beats.headline: Casting now, five minutes
beats.text: Carl gives the order: Sledge, do it. The answer comes back in the chat: one minute to chant, five minutes to cast. He is inside the castle, so he goes down with everyone else, and Ferdinand with him. Carl warns him about the zombie things, and the day of sickness, and thanks him for taking care of Donut. The Sledge's only request is that Bomo not be allowed to beat his Frogger score. Carl promises to unplug the machine.

beats.headline: The castle is gone
beats.text: Everyone hangs frozen in midair. The high elf castle is gone, and with it Signet's tattoo warriors, the changelings, a very pregnant bear who was Kiwi, and Tina, still a dinosaur, all carried off to the ninth floor. No crawlers, hunters, pets, mobs, dinosaurs, bodies or elves went with it. It took its subbasements too, so the drop is further than anyone planned. Then the world unfreezes, and they fall.

beats.headline: Landed on somebody's army
beats.text: Quasar, talking fast in front of a liaison. The castle landed in the middle of the Lemig Sortion's battlefield and splattered half their army. The ghoul things from the Zerzura spell are still a problem, but most of Carl's army got away and is installed on his battlefield, and the changelings have started on a stronghold. The Lemigs are squatting in the wrecked castle and filed a grievance calling the placement an attack. Quasar argued it was an AI action and won.

beats.headline: Tagg knows the plan
beats.text: Epitome Tagg, bargaining over Louis's brain, says he knows what they are planning with the NPC team: the Zerzura spell, to take the city of Larracos to the twelfth floor, and he intends to go with them. Carl and Donut exchange a look. The man is in the dark. He has no idea the castle has been nuked, and even if they wanted to go along with his plan, it is now impossible.

beats.headline: The second casting
beats.text: The Sledge says goodbye to Donut, and starts to cast. Five minutes. He glows. Rosetta reports that Shanty Town is inside the glow: the two towns have combined. Larracos and Shanty Town are going to the Court of the Ascendency, to land somewhere in the fields of cotton. The hired mercenaries, the Sledge among them, are expected simply to disappear. The changelings and the city's thousands of NPCs are to go. The outworlders are to be sent out of the dungeon: about 28,000 left of the more than 50,000 who came to fight. Twenty seconds, and the Sledge turns to Carl: I made a difference? You did.

beats.headline: A convent of nuns
beats.text: The goddess arrives with Huanxin driving, and the court, she says, is in a tizzy about the city these fools just teleported in. It splattered an entire convent of Resheph's nuns, and he is losing his mind. Now the zombies are wandering all over, and Odette has taken control of them, having already taken out Inpewt. The games have not even started. Behind them, Jamal stayed in the saferoom during the Zerzura, one of the few NPCs who chose to stay.

tagline.text: The punishment for failing the creeper quest: a spreading wall of thorns that boils the blood of anyone it pricks. It cannot be countered.
Timed, by Katia's math, to cover the whole map as the floor runs out, and to stop at the high elf castle.
It filled the world, stopped short of the castle, then rose into a dome over the survivors and came down on them.
Remembered on the tenth floor as the thing the crawlers loved on the sixth. Its relatives are still around.

beats.headline: The Creeping Apocalypse, failed
beats.text: The world freezes. Quest Failed. Two Odious Creepers survive, where only the hunters holed up in Zockau could reach them, so that is where it starts. First, the blood bar: saferoom time is now earned by killing. Then the punishment. The spell Gehenna Bramble has been cast, spreading at an average four and a half kilometres an hour, faster at night, slower in sun. Every plant it touches becomes a ten-metre wall of thrusting thorn vines. Pricked, your blood boils away, and you explode. It cannot be countered, poisoned or killed.

beats.headline: Beaten back, never stopped
beats.text: The rest of the rules. The brambles can be beaten back, but they are relentless. They do not come within five square metres of a stairwell. Everything else is to be encompassed, towns and buildings included, anything that is not a saferoom. Mordecai's advice arrives in the chat: Gehenna vines are dangerous, stay away from them, but if you get close, chop a few brambles off and save them. The toxin is very valuable. Don't touch the thorns. Carl, facing an angry dinosaur, answers: Not now.

beats.headline: Finished just as the timer runs out
beats.text: Carl asks Katia how far the changelings' hideout is from this Gehenna bush thing. Far, she says; they have a few days, but the Sledge's spell only works on the last day of the floor, and that is too late. She has done the math, and she is pretty sure it happened at just the right time to finish covering the map just as the timer runs out. Carl guesses where it ends. The southeast corner. Bingo: the high elf castle. The elves, he reckons, are going to try to beat the branches back.

beats.headline: The forest cries
beats.text: Signet stops to warn Carl that a darkness spreads from the north. Yes, he says, he heard: the Gehenna brambles. It has only been a few hours, and it is moving slowly, likely just reaching the borders of Zockau, more than a day from the river. It is worse than he knows, Signet says. The trees are in pain, crying for help. The trees and dryads are casting a spell of their own. It cannot stop the plague, but if it works, help may soon arrive to protect them from the worst.

beats.headline: A surprise even to us
beats.text: Seventy hours until the masquerade, and the System has an announcement. The brambles are closing in! This event was a surprise even to us. Don't let those thorns prick you! The party is still on, but because of the bramble event, nobody is to be transported back when it ends. Crawlers are instead to be let out of the castle's southern entrance, not yet infested. The elves may or may not offer safe passage after, so prepare accordingly.

beats.headline: No more suing the AI
beats.text: Zev confides, after Carl's visit with Quasar, that multiple immediately unsuccessful lawsuits followed once the brambles hit Zockau. The Syndicate Council itself, not the subcommittee but the actual council, ruled that nobody may file any more lawsuits naming the AI as a defendant, to slow the AI's deterioration. That ruling set off a whole new set of lawsuits challenging the council's authority, and the mess is working its way through the courts. Carl does not understand why they cannot just unplug the thing.

beats.headline: Exactly what we needed
beats.text: The hunters have been whittled down by more than half. The inexorable brambles combined with the blood bar seemed terrible at first, and turned out to be exactly what the crawlers needed. Most of the hunters had no idea what they were doing, were not organized or trained, and did not work well together, and between the thorns and the need to kill, they were hunted down one by one. Samantha, rolled at the hunters' anti-air guns as the workaround, was once blasted five kilometres away by one and landed in the brambles.

beats.headline: Never this aggressive
beats.text: Signet, alone on a log with a butterfly on her hand, as the sun comes up over a town the brambles are due to overtake in hours. Everything is dying, she says, but there is still beauty. She has never seen a Gehenna bramble this aggressive. It truly is the end of days. The all-tree has survived countless infestations like this one; the brambles fade with time. They are due at the elven border in a few hours, and the elves are going to spend the day beating them back. Even their magic is not enough to stop it.

beats.headline: Chasing the elves
beats.text: The Sledge, still trying to get into a tower past the rubble, reports in fragments: elves coming out of the woods, brambles chasing them, moving faster than usual. Imani confirms from outside that most crawlers there are being forced down the stairs. The brambles were not supposed to get this far into elf territory for hours yet. They seem to be reacting to the elves trying to beat them back, and since the elves at the border fell back to defend the castle, the brambles are chasing them in.

beats.headline: A dome, and a strobe
beats.text: Frozen in midair, the survivors can see it all. The brambles have filled the world and stopped about a hundred feet from where the castle was, mounted elves waiting at their edge. Thunderstruck starts playing. Then the brambles rise into a dome over the whole area and plunge it into darkness, a sickly yellow glow pulsing from little flower buds in time with the beat. The world unfreezes. As the fight falls into the castle's empty basement, the brambles push in above, entombing everyone.

beats.headline: Twenty minutes under the thorns
beats.text: Afterwards, the brambles have slowed their descent. Carl reckons twenty minutes before they are crushed, and even then the brambles are meant to form a dome over the stairwell, leaving room around it. Everyone has a treasure map of loot, all of it covered in brambles; two crawlers cast a spell and went in anyway. Carl uses his last minutes on camera for the Faction Wars election, until Zev mutes him. Everyone in the universe is now watching two crawlers fight their way through a group of brambles.

beats.headline: A cousin on the tenth floor
beats.text: Team Sparkles' biological mount is an Avernus Creeper, a gliding tangle of not-quite-sentient vines, the unicorn racer's head popping out of the top. The System's description says it is loosely related to the Gehenna Brambles you guys loved from the 6th floor: almost impossible to kill, since even a tiny branch or thorn grows rapidly to full size. Luckily this one is limited to half size and kept from procreating outside its garage. Jasha introduces the riders as Dwight and Lucienne.

entities.name: The 11th Floor Arena
entities.role: Where the audience's stand-ins go · the end of the eleventh floor's parade

tagline.text: The arena. Somewhere an audience vote can send a killed mob, or a 'stand-in' for it. The notification says nothing more.
The arena, on the eleventh floor. Kill certain mobs, let the audience vote, and either the creature survives to be sent there or a stand-in from outside the dungeon goes in its place.
The arena at the end of the parade: the crawl itself in miniature, stocked with the tenth floor's kills or their stand-ins, and a floor boss between the crawlers and the stairs.
The Arena. A dozen football fields of packed dirt around a white tree, masked stand-ins dying by the thousand, and two summons of the crawlers' choosing: Scolopendra, then Khepri.

beats.headline: A manatee's stand-in
beats.text: Princess Donut left a manatee's fate to the audience, and a notification arrives: the people have voted for Otto the slime guy to be the manatee 'stand-in' in the arena. That is all it says. Crawler Carl asks around. Others are getting similar notices; one crawler who let the audience vote on his mob is told they voted to transfer the monster to the 'arena.' Mordecai has no idea what any of it means. Per the AI's manatee lore, Otto is a registered guest of Club Scolopendra.

beats.headline: A quest that pays in stand-ins
beats.text: A new quest: reunite Dong Quixote with his best friend in the world, Corcunda, in two parts, the second needing Corcunda's other half and a fleshmancer. The reward is unlike anything else on offer. Two stand-ins of the crawlers' choosing, sent to the Arena on the 11th floor. Nobody yet knows what the Arena is. The prize has been set anyway.

beats.headline: What anyone actually knows
beats.text: Crawler Carl works the chat. Killing certain mobs on this floor offers a choice: take the experience, or let the audience vote. One way, the creature survives and is sent to the arena. The other way, a stand-in is sent, and the stand-ins seem to be people from outside the dungeon ecosystem, like guests of the resort on the eighteenth floor. The arena is on the eleventh floor. Nobody knows anything beyond that. Carl starts wondering who he could drag down there to do the most damage.

beats.headline: Eighty percent for the stand-in
beats.text: Zev reads the AI's explanation over the loudspeakers. The mobs that offer a vote are special guest creatures: made for other purposes, never used, and left in the cold. Choose vote, and the home audience either sends the creature to the 11th floor or brings a stand-in there, and they know who the stand-in is before they vote. Just about 80% of the votes have favored the stand-in. The eleventh floor itself, she announces, is a parade, a celebration, and a march to the arena.

beats.headline: Choose once inside
beats.text: Quest complete: Dong and Corcunda are reunited, with Dong still alive, and the AI asks whether anyone knows how difficult it had to make that quest to slot this prize. It is sure their plan is suicidal. The reward is confirmed. The crawlers may choose two creatures, people, whatever, within the AI's sphere of influence, to bring to the 11th floor arena waiting at the end of the Parade of Horribles. To ratchet up the drama, the choice waits until they are inside the arena. Carl sighs, and says they need to get to work.

beats.headline: The crawl, in miniature
beats.text: The floor's rules arrive, read out by Chaco, voluntold as Grand Master of the parade. Near the end of the parade route the floats pass the judging stands, and then the progression ends at an arena. The arena represents the crawl itself, and it is where the fighting finally starts: populated with monsters killed on the tenth floor or their stand-ins, along with a floor boss. Kill the boss, and the stairwell opens. Simple, he says, and admits he does not really understand it either. Prepotente points out that gods may arrive huge.

beats.headline: Stand-ins in the judging stands
beats.text: Florin sees it first: the people in the judging stands are not the masked crowd lining the route. They wear masks too, but they are tied up and struggling. Examined, each is a Stand-In, brought to the arena by audience vote; there were too many to fit inside, so some were put out here. In the front row, in a manatee mask, a slime tries to form arms and break free, and cannot. Then the airship opens its bay doors and the sluggalos rain down on the stands.

beats.headline: Welcome to the Arena
beats.text: The door is sized for Godzilla. Inside is a space the size of a dozen football fields, a white tree towering at its centre, packed dirt already running red. Thousands of monsters teleport in and fight each other. A woman in a mask flees, is torn apart by panther mobs, and is revealed as an orc: these are the remaining stand-ins, masked as the beasts they stand in for, outnumbered a hundred to one. The stairs to the 12th open on the floor boss's death. Carl's first choice: Scolopendra.

beats.headline: The second summons
beats.text: Inside Club Scolopendra, Emberus demands to know who killed his son. Two people are responsible, Crawler Carl tells him, and he is bringing them here to confess. The first is Khepri. He can explain himself, Carl says: for my second summon to the arena, I choose Khepri. He prays the god lands where the prize promised, in the arena and not in the club. Khepri enters the realm outside, giant. Carl does not actually know for certain who killed Emberus's son.

entities.name: The Horribles
entities.role: The masked crowd along the parade route

tagline.text: A Horrible. Level X. One of thousands of masked, grimy figures lining the parade route: a non-combatant who is not really there, a memory from the Eulogist.
The horribles. Memories of the Primals, then the avatars of dead mobs, watching from the arena's bleachers in silent witness to what the crawlers do next.

beats.headline: Ten deep in the fog
beats.text: The parade route is a yellow-brick road through knee-high fog, and thousands of people line it, about ten deep, facing the floats and saying nothing: adults, children, babies in arms, human or humanlike, in earthy rags as if just dug up. Every one wears an oversized, bulbous mask of a goblin, troll, hobgoblin or demon, pressed so tight the masks knock askew. There is no music. Mongo wants at them and is told to leave them alone. Donut has her Wall of Fire ready. They are said not to attack.

beats.headline: A memory from the Eulogist
beats.text: Carl examines a girl of about eight in a bright green goblin mask. A Horrible. Level X. A non-combatant, not really here because she no longer exists; under the mask, what some people call a Primal. The AI does not know her name. She is a memory from the Eulogist, it says, an anonymous inkling of what they had before ascending to post-physical form, and every one of them a small sample of what once was. I am her, and she is me. Carl, mostly, understands.

beats.headline: They flinch with the parade
beats.text: Their giant heads creak as they turn to follow the floats. When the AI, speaking through Grigori, says the word me, the world shakes, the horribles stumble, and they quickly shuffle back into position. The masked people tied up in the judging stands, Florin reports, are not them. When the AI grades the Resolution float a C and breaks every leg on it, all around the road the horribles scream in pain, one quick jolt, and are back to normal right after, as if nothing had happened.

beats.headline: The masks shatter
beats.text: When the Destruction float fires everything at once, the horribles fall over one by one, as if dead. Their masks crack like glass on the ground and they vanish into the fog, while the AI narrates the war and the nine-tier attack meant to end it. As the story reaches the Apothecary and the Syndicate repeating history, they rise again, unmasked, their faces now horrific versions of the creatures they portrayed. Examined: Marsh Troll, Level X, an avatar of a troll that died in the 3,424th season. Not really here.

beats.headline: Witnesses in the bleachers
beats.text: The arena's bleachers stand in smoky shadow, filled to capacity with silent observers: the horribles, the former mobs, dead and present only as avatars, witnessing the slaughter about to start. Carl understands the arrangement. The AI was once a Primal, a cup from the ocean, and the NPCs and mobs, goblins to gods, are drips from the same well, aggregate intelligence, peeled away, given consciousness and denied return. The monsters about to die in the arena, victims too, are soon to join them. The lost. The horribles.

beats.headline: They stand, and are gone
beats.text: The gods are gone. The monsters are dead. The horribles in the stands remain, watching. Then, as one, they all stand, still silent, still watching. Fog rises, and in moments they too are gone. What is left in the dirt are the stand-ins' blood-splattered masks: one, a fanged rabbit, reads Horribles mask, as worn by the late Gershwin Banks, CFO of Dictum Waystation Controls. Mongo and Rend lick at them. Eat the rich, says Carl.

entities.name: The Walk-On List
entities.role: Bounties on the natives a production wants

tagline.text: The Walk-On List. The names a production wants pulled from a planet's survivors, and the bounty hunters who sneak down to collect them. Illegal, and as old as the crawl itself.
The Walk-On List. Explained on Odette's show around a guest who was hunted off it, in a version of events Carl knows to be utter horseshit.

beats.headline: Sadir signs on
beats.text: For Sadir, a null with two strikes on his trespass record, the season's Walk-On List is work: he marched to the closest port and signed onto a bounty crew that hires his kind. Everybody knows about the list. The Syndicate knows. There was a holo drama about it. Rights organisations write bills demanding it be condemned, and nothing ever happens: Syndicate security still hunts trespassers, and the corporations who are the real culprits face no accountability at all. He has children in a null commune to keep.

beats.headline: Collected, Crawlers, Natives
beats.text: How it works. A planetwide collection sorts everyone into the Collected, caught in the collapse; the Crawlers, who went in; and the Natives, everybody else. Producers may pull collected people into the show for drama. Natives are untouchable under the rules. So, the list: trackers hired to sneak onto the planet and kidnap survivors a production wants. Not remotely legal; as old as the crawl. Earth's natives had their implants scrambled when the crawl began, and Borant's early start left the records two days stale.

beats.headline: A cat called Gravy Boat
beats.text: This season's list is shorter than usual, and competition is fierce. Dozens of hunters search a tropical zone a tsunami washed clean for one high-value woman; as many hunt a little girl's father in the southern hemisphere. Sometimes a list has 5,000 names and one or two are found. Sadir and his sac partner Gennrik are after a cat named Gravy Boat, an A-tier target, with a bonus for the first capture, in a survivors' camp in what was once Seattle.

beats.headline: Lexis gets there first
beats.text: The raid goes wrong once the tent is open. Gennrik's chest explodes; Sadir, hands up, stares at the woman on the mattress and asks, Beatrice? Lexis takes her. Odette's orders for the scene: make it look like a fight over the cat, buy out the null's warrant to keep him quiet, let the wounded human expire, and have a security man sneak the cat over to Borant so the walk-on bounty gets collected. Beatrice is to be reassured: no selling her to Borant. They have a better use for her.

beats.headline: The version for broadcast
beats.text: Odette's show runs a segment Carl and Donut are not allowed to see: the rules for humans who stayed out of the dungeon, and the walk-on list, the illegal practice of bounty hunters finding survivors to sell to the production. Then Odette's story: a guest who survived the collapse, was kidnapped by bounty hunters and taken off world, until Borant, wanting no part of kidnapping, turned the pirates over to the Syndicate. A pirate died. She is now a full citizen. Carl knows it for utter horseshit. The guest is Beatrice.

beats.headline: What they could have used
beats.text: Waiting to face whatever this floor has built out of his past, Carl turns it over. These replicants are not the real people, not if they were crushed in the collapse. But he remembers what Odette told them about the walk-on list, where they took people who had survived. They would have used Bea as Queen Imogen, given the opportunity, and that would really have been her. Whatever they are about to face, he keeps telling himself, is not the real thing.

beats.headline: A debate reignited
beats.text: Opening the warlord council, Odette runs through the seven teams still standing. For the first time ever, one is a crawler team, and one is an NPC team, led by Warlords Ferdinand, whose existence, she says, has reignited debate about the controversial walk-on list, and dungeon-born Juice Box, who in theory should not even know she is in a game. She does not say more about the list. She moves straight on to the showrunner at the table.
